title: Conservative (Masorti) Judaism
hookLine: halakha as binding, and developing through history

lines: DEBTS RELEASED IN THE SEVENTH YEAR.
cards: Every seventh year, the Torah says, debts are released. A generous law. But the Mishnah tells what happened next: as the seventh year drew near, people stopped lending to the poor, afraid they would never be repaid.
The Torah had warned against exactly that, the thought in the heart that says the year of release is at hand.

So Hillel, the great sage, enacted the prozbul, a court document that kept loans collectible, so that lending would go on. The goal of the law was kept by changing how it worked. Today's movement points to that story.

teach.b: Masorti. It's the Hebrew word for traditional, from masoret, tradition. In North America the movement is called Conservative Judaism; in Israel and elsewhere, Masorti.
First, halakha is binding. Conservative Judaism holds that Jewish law obligates Jews: Shabbat, kashrut, prayer, the festivals. That sets it apart from movements that see the law as guidance only.
Second, the law has a history. Conservative scholars study how halakha grew: the Bible, the Mishnah, the Talmud, the codes, each generation adding and adjusting.
They point to moments like Hillel's prozbul, where sages changed how a law worked in order to keep its purpose.

Third, so the law can still develop. If it developed before, the movement holds, it may develop now, carefully, by rabbis trained in the sources, reasoning from inside the tradition, with history in view.
Orthodox Judaism also answers new questions from inside the law, as you heard; the difference is in how far change may go, and who may make it. Fourth, the deep root.
The tractate of the Fathers opens: Moses received the Torah and handed it on, masar, to Joshua. Masoret, tradition, is something handed on.

teach.h: ASK THY FATHER, AND HE WILL SHEW THEE.
teach.b: Deuteronomy says: "ask thy father, and he will shew thee; thy elders, and they will tell thee." The movement hears in that a tradition both received and alive, passing through human hands, and shaped by them.
Tomorrow, how those hands actually make decisions.

how: Conservative and Masorti Jews hold halakha as binding while studying its historical development, and their rabbis rule on new questions from the traditional sources with that history in view.

games.q: you're Hillel. a law meant to help the poor is making people stop lending to them. what do you do?
o: enact a court document that keeps loans collectible, so lending goes on.
leave it; the law is the law.
games.why: he enacted the prozbul. the purpose of the law, care for the poor, was kept by changing how it worked.

practice: Bring to mind one habit or rule you started for a good reason: a budget, a morning routine, a house rule about phones at dinner.

Ask what it was for, and whether, like the year of release, it has started working against its own aim. If it has, picture one small change that would serve the purpose better, the way Hillel's court document kept lending alive.
